summary.text:
A well-structured strategy from a council that is currently a NET INVESTOR by £62.3m -- £179.3m of investments at 4.31% against £117.0m of borrowing at 4.11% -- and that expects to move sharply the other way. The liability benchmark trebles from £57.1m to £188.1m in three years, driven by the Loans CFR growing £87m while balance-sheet resources shrink £44m. The strategy plans NO new external borrowing in 2026/27 and instead runs internal borrowing up 4x from £37.6m to £150.9m.

The distinctive feature is a full MRP policy change from straight-line to annuity, retrospective to 1 April 2025 within FY 2025/26 (Section 3.2 of the covering report). Saving £1.667m in 2025/26 and "up to £30 million over the next 10 years" in the paper's own words. Same £284.55m total MRP over 50 years, front-loading eased into the back-loading -- the 1-10 year MRP drops £30m; the 21-50 year MRP rises £33m. Uses the PWLB certainty rate at 1 April 2025 in the annuity calculation. Rationale spelled out unusually plainly, including the honest rider that overall interest costs are slightly higher because principal is repaid more slowly.

Loan-book reconciliation ties tightly: our file holds 26 PWLB loans totalling £111,122,500 at 4.0938% against their £111.1m at 4.13% (Table 1 p.11, footnote confirming PWLB composition at p.26). Weighted rate 0.04 percentage points apart -- effective-interest accounting typically explains that. Balance-sheet identity ties across all four forecast years (Table 7 and Table 1.2.4). The book is distinctly LONG-DATED: only £10.4m matures inside two years (8.9%), against Medway's £245m or Northumberland's £121m in the same bucket. The £15m 2058 PWLB at 2.62% sits at an indicative £6.5m discount and drives most of the £9.8m mark-to-market gap on the book.

The Arlingclose interest-rate forecast (December 2025) called for two further quarter-point cuts to Bank Rate of 3.25% by end-2026 -- Bank Rate is still 3.75% and the SONIA/OIS curve now prices it above 4% within a year.

officer.subject: Your MRP switch to annuity, and £57m to £188m in three years
officer.body:
Hi Melanie,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 that went to Cabinet on 11 February and to Council on 24 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The paper is unusually clearly structured and the MRP rationale is one of the more candid we've read, so this is offered in that spirit.

A reconciliation first. Our PWLB file holds 26 loans totalling £111,122,500 at a weighted 4.09%, against the £111.1m at 4.13% in your Table 1 and the £111.1m PWLB figure your paragraph 1.2.5 footnote picks out from the £145.0m long-term year-end composition. Principal ties to about £22,500; the 0.04 point rate gap is what effective-interest accounting on premium and discount adjustments usually produces. Your balance-sheet identity in Table 7 ties across all four forecast years too — 205.2 less 167.6 leaves 37.6 internal at 31 March 2026, and the same subtraction reproduces to 57.3, 99.6 and 150.9 across the outer years.

The MRP change in Section 3.2 is the most distinctive thing in the paper. Moving both pre-2008 supported and post-2008 prudential borrowing from straight-line to annuity, retrospective to 1 April 2025, saves £1.667m in the current year alone — 2025/26 MRP falls from £9,900k to £8,233k, mostly on the post-2008 line (£6,222k to £4,925k). Over 50 years the paper's own profile keeps the same £284.55m total but shifts £30.0m of MRP out of the 1-10 year bucket into years 21-50. Using the PWLB certainty rate at 1 April 2025 in the annuity calculation is what unlocks the "up to £30 million over the next 10 years" your paper quotes on p.4. It is worth noting how few councils spell out the trade-off as plainly as your rationale does — "overall costs are slightly higher when using the annuity method as the principal is repaid more slowly resulting in higher overall interest costs" is exactly the honest framing that goes missing in most MRP change reports we have read.

Behind that policy change sits the shape in your Table 1.2.4. The liability benchmark grows from £57.1m at 31 March 2026 to £188.1m by 31 March 2029 — the net loans requirement widens from £7.1m to £138.1m over the same window. Balance-sheet resources fall £43.9m while Loans CFR rises £87.1m. Coupled with the borrowing strategy in paragraph 4.32 that recommends no external borrowing in 2026/27, internal borrowing has to do the work: £37.6m today growing to £150.9m in three years. Which means the council moves from where you are now — a £62.3m net investor with £179.3m of investments earning 4.31% against £117.0m of borrowing at 4.11% — to needing meaningful external borrowing before 2028/29. That is a lot of shape change to sit inside one strategy period, and it is why the mid-year and outturn reads will matter more than usual this cycle.

One small piece of data if it is useful. The Arlingclose December 2025 forecast at paragraph 4.29 had Bank Rate falling to 3.25% by end-2026 — two more quarter-point cuts on top of the December cut. Six months on, Bank Rate is still 3.75%, the MPC has not cut again, and the SONIA/OIS curve now prices Bank Rate above 4% at the one-year point. The long end is roughly 0.5 to 0.6 points higher than the day Cabinet took the strategy. That is more a data point for the next update than a surprise — the strategy already flags rate volatility at paragraph 4.30 — but the direction of travel matters for the internal-versus-external calculus your paragraph 4.32 sets out. The full curve and SONIA path are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard, and every council's PWLB book priced against today's DMO discount curve is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. For context our engine currently prices your book at about £9.8m indicative discount against £111.1m — driven mostly by the £15m 2058 PWLB at 2.62% which shows an indicative £6.5m of it. Indicative only, only the DMO can quote, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment on top.

Three courses fit. Reading the PWLB certainty curve covers the mechanics of what has moved since your Cabinet took this strategy. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given where your own benchmark is heading and CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates. MRP: methods and choices is the one that would sit closest to the Section 3.2 change if you or Mark wanted to run through the alternatives. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
